extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/epistemology (general readers, undergraduates, and scholars studying Locke or theories of mind)
extracted.subtask_description: Close-exposition of faculties of the mind (perception, retention/memory, discernment, composition, naming, abstraction) as presented in a classical philosophy text, describing how ideas are received, retained, and manipulated. Useful for readers studying early modern epistemology and cognitive accounts of idea-formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception as the primary inlet of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception (by sensation and reflection) is the FIRST step and degree towards knowledge and the inlet of all the materials of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception furnishes the simple ideas from which the mind builds knowledge. The fewer and duller the senses and impressions, the more remote a creature is from human-like knowledge. Use this as a foundational principle: evaluate cognitive status by the number, vividness, and variety of perceptual inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sight-specific judgments and susceptibility to error
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas received by sight are apt to be mistaken for direct perception because sight conveys many distinct ideas (light, colours, space, figure, motion) which we habitually use to judge one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that learned associations and frequent co-occurrence can make a judgment formed by inference feel like direct sensation. Example/anti-pattern: confusing a quick, habitual inference (e.g., identifying an object by its color/shape) with immediate perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit converts ideas of sensation into ideas of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: By custom and repeated experience the mind unconsciously changes sensory ideas into judgments, so that one (sensation) excites the other (judgment) often without notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the role of practiced associations in producing rapid 'judgments' that bypass conscious noticing of the originating sensation. This explains why skilled or experienced agents may respond correctly yet be unable to state the sensory basis of their response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception as the faculty distinguishing animals from plants
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception is the faculty that puts the distinction between animals and vegetables; plants' motions are mechanistic, not indicative of sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capacity for perception (not mere mechanical response) as a criterion when attributing sensation or rudimentary cognition to organisms. Consider degree and adaptiveness of perception relative to the organism's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception varies by species and condition
rubrics_metrics.description: All animals have perception in some degree, but the number and acuity of senses and the clarity of impressions differ according to species and an organism’s condition (e.g., oysters vs humans; decrepit old age reduces perception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate perceptual capability contextually: consider ecological needs, mobility, and bodily condition (age, disease) when judging the usefulness or presence of perceptual faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention (memory) — contemplation and revival
rubrics_metrics.description: Retention is the faculty that keeps simple ideas received from sensation or reflection, either by keeping an idea actually in view (contemplation) or by reviving ideas that have disappeared (memory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between active contemplation (ideas held in present view) and memory (revival of past perceptions). Memory is described as a power to revive perceptions plus the additional perception that 'it has had them before.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors that fix ideas in memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention, repetition, and the accompaniment of pleasure or pain help fix ideas in memory; ideas repeatedly refreshed or conveyed by multiple channels are most tenacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To strengthen retention, employ focused attention, repetition, multimodal presentation, and emotional salience. Examples: primary qualities and frequent bodily sensations (solidity, extension, heat) are seldom lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas fade: causes of oblivion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas that are lightly impressed, not repeated, or produced only once often fade and can be entirely lost; bodily constitution (disease, fever) can also erase ideas from memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for decay of memory over time and the role of bodily/physiological factors. Anti-pattern: assuming that early impressions remain without refreshment — they can vanish like 'shadows' if not renewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory can be active or passive; will aids retrieval
rubrics_metrics.description: In remembering, the mind often actively searches for hidden ideas; ideas can also arise spontaneously or be roused by passions, and upon revival the mind recognizes them as formerly imprinted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat retrieval as sometimes voluntary (search-driven) and sometimes involuntary (cue-driven). Emotional states can trigger the revival of dormant ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two principal defects of memory: oblivion and slowness
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory has two defects: losing ideas entirely (oblivion) and moving slowly in retrieving stored ideas (slowness), the latter producing effects akin to stupidity when severe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate memory performance both for completeness of storage and for retrieval speed. Functionally, stored ideas unavailable in time of need are of little use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing and the formation of relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing ideas (in respect of extent, degree, time, place, etc.) is a mental operation that underlies the class of ideas called Relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparison to form relational ideas; this faculty enables abstract reasoning about relations and is crucial for general reasoning beyond immediate sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition (compounding/enlarging) to make complex ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind composes several simple ideas into complex ones and can enlarge by aggregating similar units (e.g., units to a dozen), enabling concepts like number and complex properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess complex ideas as constructions from simpler ideas via composition/enlargement. Brutes likely compound far less; humans uniquely form many complex ideas by active composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming: words as outward marks of internal ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Words (signs) stand as outward marks of internal ideas; children learn to use verbal signs to signify ideas to others, borrowing or inventing names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize naming as social and cognitive: names allow communication and categorization. Evaluate adequacy of a sign by its stability and shared use for conveying the underlying idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction and the formation of general ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstraction makes particular ideas general by considering their appearance separate from time, place, and circumstances; this produces universal ideas and general names applicable across instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat abstraction as a distinctively human operation that permits universals and language. Brutes lack abstraction (no use of general signs), which Locke posits as the key distinction between human and animal cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and varieties of human intellect (idiots, madmen, prodigies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in faculties (perception, retention, composition, etc.) explain cognitive variations: idiots lack quickness/activity; madmen join ideas wrongly (reasoning correctly from false premises); prodigies may have exceptional retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing cognitive abilities, distinguish between loss of faculty (inability to form propositions) and disorderly use of faculties (false combinations). Examples: Pascal's prodigious memory vs. degrees of madness producing consistent but false inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological claim: appeal to experience and the 'dark room' metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: The author appeals to experience and observation as the method for discovering how ideas are brought into the understanding, likening the understanding to a dark room illuminated by small openings (sensation/reflection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt empirically grounded inquiry: base claims about mind and knowledge on observation of human minds in different ages, educations, and conditions rather than on assumed innate ideas.
